content: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic medication that has been shown to be superior in treating refractory schizophrenia, particularly in reducing movement disorders. However, its use is associated with a significant risk of serious blood disorders, such as agranulocytosis, which can be potentially fatal. In recent years, newer atypical antipsychotics have been developed with the aim of achieving better tolerability and improved effectiveness. The objective of this review was to compare the clinical effects of clozapine with other atypical antipsychotics, including amisulpride, aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, sertindole, ziprasidone, and zotepine, in the treatment of schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared clozapine with these other medications in any dose or oral formulation. The review analyzed data from 27 blinded RCTs involving 3,099 participants. Twelve trials compared clozapine with olanzapine, five with quetiapine, nine with risperidone, one with ziprasidone, and two with zotepine. Attrition rates were high across the studies, with an overall dropout rate of 30.1%, which complicates the interpretation of the results. Clozapine had a higher dropout rate due to adverse effects compared to olanzapine (9 RCTs, 1,674 participants; relative risk [RR] 1.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07 to 2.40; number needed to harm [NNH] 25, CI 15 to 73) and risperidone (6 RCTs, 627 participants; RR 1.88, CI 1.11 to 3.21; NNH 16, CI 9 to 59). However, fewer participants in the clozapine groups discontinued treatment due to inefficacy compared to risperidone (6 RCTs, 627 participants; RR 0.40, CI 0.23 to 0.70; number needed to treat [NNT] 11, CI 7 to 21), suggesting that clozapine may have higher efficacy in some cases. Clozapine was more effective than zotepine in improving general mental state, as measured by the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) total score (1 RCT, 59 participants; mean difference [MD] -6.00, CI -9.83 to -2.17). However, clozapine was not consistently more effective than olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, or ziprasidone in improving general mental state. There was no significant difference between clozapine and olanzapine or risperidone in addressing positive or negative symptoms of schizophrenia. Interestingly, two studies from China suggested that quetiapine was more effective than clozapine in treating negative symptoms (2 RCTs, 142 participants; MD 2.23, CI 0.99 to 3.48). Clozapine caused fewer extrapyramidal side effects compared to risperidone (6 RCTs, 304 participants; RR 0.39, CI 0.22 to 0.68; NNT 7, CI 5 to 18) and zotepine (59 participants; RR 0.05, CI 0.00 to 0.86; NNT 3, CI 2 to 5). However, clozapine was associated with a higher incidence of decreased white blood cell counts compared to olanzapine, as well as more hypersalivation and sedation compared to olanzapine, risperidone, and quetiapine. Additionally, clozapine caused more seizures than olanzapine and risperidone and was linked to significant weight gain, which was not observed with risperidone. Other adverse effects were less well-documented but included the following: clozapine did not alter prolactin levels, unlike olanzapine, risperidone, and zotepine. Compared to quetiapine, clozapine was associated with a higher incidence of electrocardiogram (ECG) abnormalities. Clozapine also caused a greater increase in triglyceride levels compared to quetiapine and risperidone. Furthermore, clozapine appeared to improve social functioning less effectively than risperidone. However, fewer participants in the clozapine group required hospitalization to prevent suicide attempts compared to those on olanzapine. Important outcomes such as service use, cognitive functioning, satisfaction with care, and quality of life were rarely reported in the included studies. The authors concluded that clozapine may be slightly more effective than zotepine and risperidone, but further trials are needed to confirm these findings. The distinct side-effect profile of clozapine compared to other second-generation antipsychotics may play a critical role in treatment selection, depending on the clinical context and patient preferences. However, the high dropout rates in the studies limit the validity and generalizability of these findings. Further large, well-designed trials are necessary to address gaps in knowledge, particularly regarding cognitive functioning, quality of life, mortality, and healthcare service use.
